title: Choose an API evolution strategy for three client versions
description: Design an API versioning and deprecation strategy that supports a v1 mobile app, v2 web app, and an upcoming v3 redesign without breaking existing clients.

data.text: Your public API has 1,200 enterprise clients. You are shipping a v3 redesign that removes two deprecated fields and changes the response envelope. The v1 mobile app is still used by 30 percent of users. You need a migration strategy that lets all three versions coexist for 18 months without breaking contracts.

terms.definition: A strategy for managing breaking changes while keeping old clients functional.
A contract promise that newer versions do not break consumers of older versions.
A published timeline and process for retiring an API version.
Using headers (Accept, API-Version) rather than URLs to select the API version.
A toggle that enables or disables functionality at runtime without deployment.

data.title: The compatibility trap
data.text: Every 'small breaking change' accumulates. Without a formal versioning policy and deprecation timeline, you end up maintaining N versions indefinitely because you never gave clients a hard deadline.

data.title: URL versioning, header versioning, and GraphQL

cards.title: URL Versioning
pros: Visually obvious which version a client is calling
Simple to deprecate: return 404 on old paths
CDN caching works naturally per path
cons: URL proliferation: N versions times N endpoints
Code duplication or adapter layers to share logic
Clients must change URLs when upgrading
Does not compose well with media-type versioning

cards.title: Header Versioning
cards.description: Version via Accept or a custom API-Version header.
pros: Single URL per resource; versions are negotiable
Easier to route at the gateway level
cons: Less visible in logs and browser history
Caching proxies require Vary header configuration
Harder for clients to test manually

cards.title: GraphQL Federation
cards.description: Schema evolution through field deprecation and type extensions.
pros: Clients select exactly the fields they need
Deprecation warnings are visible in schema introspection
Additive changes are non-breaking by default
cons: Removing a field breaks any client that still requests it
Query complexity limits add operational overhead
Requires all clients to migrate to GraphQL
Not suitable for simple public REST APIs

data.title: HTTP: Sunset header for deprecation signaling
data.content: Inform clients of version retirement without breaking them immediately.
data.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
API-Version: 1
Sunset: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 23:59:59 GMT
Deprecation: true
Link: </v2/users>; rel="successor-version"

Body (v1 format):
{
  "id": "123",
  "username": "alice",
  "email": "a@b.com"
}

data.title: v2 adds new fields without removing v1 fields
data.content: Old clients continue to work; new fields are ignored by v1 clients.

items.text: How many active client versions must be supported simultaneously?
Do you control all clients, or are they third-party integrations?
Can you enforce client upgrade timelines via support contracts?
Is your API surface small and stable, or rapidly evolving?
Do you have automated contract testing between API and clients?

data.caption: Version lifecycle: active, deprecated, sunset
data.definition:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active
    Active --> Deprecated: Announce sunset date
    Deprecated --> Sunset: Date arrives
    Sunset --> [*]: Disabled
    note right of Deprecated
        Returns Sunset header
        New clients guided to v2
    end note

data.title: Recommended approach: URL versioning with Sunset headers
data.content: Use /v1, /v2, /v3 paths. Each version lives in its own controller or folder, sharing business logic through internal services. Publish a 12-month sunset timeline and enforce it through automated monitoring. v1 clients that have not migrated by the sunset date receive 301 redirects to a migration guide.

data.title: Testing backward compatibility
data.text: Use Pact or similar consumer-driven contract testing. Every breaking change should fail a contract test before it reaches production. If you cannot test it, do not ship it.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Versioning is a social contract backed by headers and automated tests.
Deprecation without a hard sunset date is just nostalgia.
Share logic through internal services, not through versioned controllers.
data.takeaway: Give clients a clear upgrade path, enforce it with automation, and remove old versions on schedule.
